questions.question: Which of the following statements about cardiac jelly is incorrect?

options.A: Provide structural support during early heart development
options.B: Facilitates end-systolic occlusion, improving pumping efficiency
options.C: Store elastic energy during systole for the refilling phase of the heart.
options.D: Cellular matrix secreted by the endocardium in the developing heart.

explanation.text: The cardiac jelly is an acellular matrix that is secreted by the myocardium in the developing heart. Cardiac Jelly (CJ): A gelatinous, cell-free extracellular matrix filling the myoendocardial space of the embryonic heart tube.

Function: Acts as a hydraulic skeleton, providing structural support during early heart development. (Option A) Facilitates end-systolic occlusion of the embryonic heart lumen, improving pumping efficiency. (Option B) Stores elastic energy during systole, aiding the refilling phase of the heart. (Option C)

questions.question: In the image depicting fetal heart development, which structures are labelled as A and B, respectively?

options.A: A: Ostium primum, B: Ostium secundum
options.B: A: Foramen ovale, B: Ostium primum
options.C: A: Septum primum, B: Septum secundum
options.D: A: Septum secundum, B: Septum primum

explanation.text: Septum primum (Label A) grows first and contributes to the division of the atria. The septum secundum (Label B) grows later and overlaps the septum primum, forming the foramen ovale, which allows right-to-left blood flow in fetal life. Septum Primum Formed as a sickle-shaped fold from the roof and dorsal wall of the primitive atrium due to pressure from the bulbus cordis.

Grows downward toward the atrioventricular (AV) canal and septum intermedium, fusing with the latter. Ostium Primum Before the septum primum reaches and fuses with the septum intermedium, a gap (foramen primum) allows blood flow between the right and left atria. Ostium Secundum Upper part of the septum primum breaks down, creating a new gap (foramen secundum) before the foramen primum closes. The septum primum now has a free upper edge.

Septum Secundum Grows down from the roof of the atrial chamber, to the right of the septum primum, overlapping the free upper edge of the septum primum as it grows. Foramen Ovale Formation Overlapping septa create the foramen ovale, allowing blood to flow from right to left atrium during fetal life, preventing left-to-right flow. Patent throughout fetal life.

Obliteration of Foramen Ovale Post-birth, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, increasing pressure in this chamber greater than the right atrium, causing fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale. Annulus ovalis (adults) corresponds to the lower free edge of the septum secundum, while the fossa ovalis represents the septum primum.

questions.question: A 5-year-old patient is diagnosed with an atrial septal defect (ASD) characterized by a large opening between the left and right atria. Which embryological defect is most commonly associated with this significant type of ASD?

options.B: Ostium secundum defect
options.C: Sinus venosus defect

explanation.text: Ostium secundum defect is the most common significant ASD characterized by a large atrial opening. Defects in Interatrial Septal Development Atrial Septal Defect (ASD): Varies from total absence of the atrial septum to small openings, such as probe patency of the oval foramen. Most significant defect: Ostium secundum defect, characterized by a large opening between the left and right atria.

Causes: Excessive cell death and resorption of the septum primum. Inadequate development of the septum secundum. Complete Absence of Atrial Septum: Known as common atrium or cor triloculare biventriculare. Result from complete failure of the septum primum and septum secundum to form. Premature Closure of Foramen Ovale: It can occur during prenatal life. Results in: Massive hypertrophy of the right atrium and ventricle.
Underdevelopment of the left side of the heart. Often leads to death shortly after birth.
**Ostium primum defect (Option A):** Accounts for about 10% of septal defects and develops due to a deficiency in tissue near the atrioventricular valves, making it less common than ostium secundum.

**Sinus venosus defect (Option B):** is located outside the fossa ovalis on the right septal surface. It is associated with anomalous right upper pulmonary venous return rather than a large atrial opening between the atria.

**Coronary Sinus Defect (Option C):** is located in the wall separating the coronary sinus from the left atrium; it may be fenestrated or absent and does not create a significant opening between the left and right atria.

questions.question: During an echocardiogram, a raised ridge is observed around a depression on the interatrial septum. Which structure is most likely involved?

options.B: Septum secundum
options.C: Fossa ovalis

explanation.text: Limbus fossa ovalis is the raised ridge surrounding the fossa ovalis. Fossa Ovalis: (Option C) Depressed area located in the lower portion of the right atrial side of the interatrial septum. Remnant of the foramen ovale. Septum primum which is on the left atrial side, forms the floor of the fossa ovalis. Limbus Fossa Ovalis: (Option D) A raised ridge (annulus) that surrounds the perimeter of the fossa ovalis.
It is formed from the septum secundum, an infolding of the atrial roof.
**Septum primum (Option A):** forms the floor of the fossa ovalis, not the raised ridge surrounding it.
**Septum secundum (Option B):** contributes to the formation of the limbus fossa ovalis but does not directly appear as a raised ridge itself.

questions.question: During the spiraling process of the septum, what anatomical change occurs in relation to the pulmonary trunk and aorta?

options.B: The aorta moves to the right side of the body.
options.C: The pulmonary trunk crosses anteriorly and to the left of the aorta.
options.D: There is no change in the position of either vessel.

explanation.text: The spiraling of the aorticopulmonary septum positions the pulmonary trunk anteriorly and to the left of the aorta. This arrangement is crucial for separating the pulmonary and systemic circulations. The bulbus cordis

elongates into three segments: Proximal part forms bulboventricular chamber Middle part: Conus cordis (outflow tract) Distal part (Truncus arteriosus) develops into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk Truncus arteriosus undergoes septation and spiraling. There are two swellings along the truncus arteriosus- truncal swellings distally and conal swellings proximally.

The truncal swellings, resembling endocardial cushions, divide the lumen into the proximal ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk. The fusion of truncal and conal swellings establishes the pulmonary trunk’s origin from the right ventricle and the aorta’s origin from the left ventricle, with aortopulmonary valves forming at these fusion lines.

Spiraling of the septum allows the pulmonary trunk to cross anterior and to the left of the aorta. (Option C) Failure of neural crest cells to migrate or disruptions to the aorticopulmonary septum leads to congenital heart disease Septation defects: Persistent truncus arteriosus: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form Tetralogy of Fallot: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the aorticopulmonary septum Comprises four defects linked to abnormalities: VSD Overriding aorta Pulmonary stenosis Right ventricular hypertrophy Double outlet right ventricle Spiraling defects: Transposition of the great vessels: Positions of the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched due to errors in truncus arteriosus division.
**The pulmonary trunk moves posteriorly (Option A):** The pulmonary trunk moves anteriorly.

**The aorta moves to the right side of the body (Option B):** The aorta does end up in a more rightward position relative to the pulmonary trunk, but it does not specifically move to the right side of the body.
**There is no change in the position of either vessel (Option D):** The spiraling process specifically reorganizes the positions of the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

questions.question: A newborn presents with significant cyanosis and a single large vessel exiting the heart on imaging studies. The echocardiogram shows a defect in the interventricular septum.What embryological failure led to this condition?

options.A: Failure of the atrioventricular septum to form.
options.B: Failure of the conotruncal ridges to form.
options.C: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral.

explanation.text: In this scenario, the newborn exhibits significant cyanosis and a single large vessel which is suggestive of persistent truncus arteriosus. It resulted from the failure of the conotruncal ridges to develop, which prevents the proper division of the outflow tracts into the aorta and pulmonary artery, leading to the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

Aorticopulmonary septum anomalies: 1) Tetralogy of Fallot: Most common conotruncal heart defect. Cause: Due to unequal division of the conus and anterior displacement of the septum. (Option D) Features four cardiovascular issues: Pulmonary infundibular stenosis Overriding aorta Ventricular septal defect (VSD) Right ventricular hypertrophy Tetralogy along with ASD is known as pentalogy of fallot.

Common in individuals with Alagille syndrome (also features liver abnormalities and distinctive facial traits). Often associated with a JAG1 gene mutation affecting neural crest cells. 2) Persistent Truncus Arteriosus: Cause: Failure of conotruncal ridges to form. (Option B) Features: Leads to a single outflow tract and a defective interventricular septum. The truncus overrides both ventricles.

Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood combine, with lung-bound blood entering systemic circulation.Results in congenital cyanotic heart disease. 3) Transposition of the Great Vessels: Cause: Occurs when the conotruncal septum fails to spiral correctly. (Option C) Features:s Aorta connects to the right ventricle, pulmonary artery connects to the left ventricle.

Patients cannot survive because deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cavae, then flows to the right ventricle and into the ascending aorta, bypassing the lungs completely. PDA is essential for survival, allowing blood flow to the lungs for oxygenation.
**Failure of the atrioventricular septum to form (Option A):** refers to atrioventricular septal defects, which involve issues in the separation of the atria and ventricles, not the outflow tracts.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the development of the interventricular septum is incorrect?

options.A: Muscular part grows from the floor of the bulboventricular cavity
options.B: Bulbar part forms from the fusion of two bulbar ridges.
options.C: Posterior part of the membranous septum separates the right ventricle from the left atrium.
options.D: Interventricular foramen forms above the muscular septum.

explanation.text: The posterior part of the membranous septum separates the left ventricle from the right atrium, not the right ventricle from the left atrium. Formation of Interventricular Septum: The interventricular septum consists

of three parts: Muscular part Bulbar part Membranous part 1. Muscular Part: Septum grows upward from the floor of the bulboventricular cavity, dividing it into right and left halves. (Option A) This growth is driven by passive dilation and hemodynamic forces. Septum fuses with the atrioventricular (AV) cushions (septum intermedium).

Interventricular foramen forms between the two ventricles at the upper margin of the septum and is eventually closed by the septum intermedium and proximal bulbar septum. (Option D) 2. Bulbar Part: Two bulbar ridges (right and left) arise from the wall of the bulboventricular cavity. These ridges fuse to form the proximal bulbar septum, which grows downward toward the muscular septum but leaves a gap. (Option B) 3.

Membranous Part: The gap between the muscular septum and the bulbar septum is filled by tissue from the AV cushions and bulbar ridges. Membranous septum consists of: Anterior part: Separates the right and left ventricles.

Posterior part: Separates the left ventricle from the right atrium. (Option C) Mechanism of Septal Formation: Interventricular septum is likely formed by the downward enlargement of the right and left ventricular cavities on either side of the septum, rather than by active septal growth itself.

questions.question: In fetal circulation, which structure allows oxygenated blood to bypass the lungs and directly enter the systemic circulation, ensuring oxygen delivery to the fetal brain and upper body?

options.B: Ductus arteriosus
options.C: Foramen ovale

explanation.text: Ductus arteriosus allows most blood from the right ventricle to bypass the lungs by shunting it directly into the aorta, ensuring efficient delivery of oxygenated blood to the fetal brain and upper body.

Fetal Circulation: Oxygenated Blood Flow: Placenta → Umbilical Vein → Ductus Venosus (bypasses liver) → Inferior Vena Cava → Right Atrium → Foramen Ovale → Left Atrium → Left Ventricle → Ascending Aorta → Oxygen to head, neck, and upper limbs Deoxygenated Blood Flow: Superior Vena Cava (SVC) → Right Atrium → Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Trunk → Ductus Arteriosus (bypass pulmonary circulation) → Descending Aorta → Lower body → Umbilical Arteries → Placenta (for oxygenation) Peculiarities of Fetal Circulation: Ductus Venosus: Directs blood to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver and preserving oxygen content. (Option A) Foramen Ovale: Allows equal distribution of blood to both sides of the heart, ensuring more oxygenated blood reaches vital organs in the upper body. (Option C) Ductus Arteriosus: Directs blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs and allowing blood to flow to the placenta for oxygenation. (Option B) More oxygenated blood flows to the upper limbs, resulting in longer upper limbs compared to lower limbs in the fetus.

**Umbilical vein (Option D):** carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus, but it doesn’t play a role in shunting blood past the lungs. Its function is to deliver oxygenated blood to the fetal circulation through the ductus venosus.

questions.question: A 3-day-old neonate presents with cyanosis, rapid breathing, and a machinery-like murmur on auscultation. Echocardiography reveals a left-to-right shunt at the level of the great vessels. Which of the following fetal circulatory changes is most likely responsible for this presentation?

options.B: Patent ductus arteriosus
options.C: Closure of ductus venosus

explanation.text: . A machinery-like murmur in a neonate along with cyanosis and rapid breathing suggests patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). PDA is a fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta that normally closes soon after birth. If it remains open (patent), it causes a left-to-right shunt (oxygenated blood from the aorta flows back into the pulmonary artery), leading to volume overload in the lungs, causing cyanosis and respiratory distress.

Persistent foramen ovale typically causes a different murmur and shunting pattern; closure of ductus venosus affects liver blood flow; malrotation of great arteries affects vessel positioning, not shunting or murmur. Changes in the Circulation at Birth: Umbilical Arteries Thick muscle walls of the umbilical arteries contract immediately after birth, occluding their lumen. This prevents the loss of fetal blood into the placenta.

Umbilical Vein and Ductus Venosus Lumen of the umbilical vein and ductus venosus occludes a few minutes after birth, allowing time for fetal blood from the placenta to return to the fetus. Ductus Arteriosus Closes initially due to muscle contraction in the vessel wall, and later, intimal proliferation permanently obliterates the lumen, redirecting blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.

Pulmonary Vessels Increase in size, allowing more blood to reach the left atrium from the lungs, increasing left atrial pressure. Foramen Ovale Increased pressure in the left atrium (due to lung circulation) and reduced pressure in the right atrium (due to cessation of placental blood flow) lead to the closure of the valve of the foramen ovale.

Fetal Circulatory Shunts and Their Changes After Birth Fetal Structure Function During Fetal Life Remnant Ductus arteriosus Shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing pulmonary circulation.

Ligamentum arteriosum Foramen ovale Shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium Fossa ovalis Ductus venosus Shunts blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver Ligamentum venosum Umbilical vein Carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus Ligamentum teres hepatis Umbilical arteries Carries deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta Proximal part: Superior vesical artery Distal part: Medial umbilical ligaments Persistent foramen ovale (Option A) allows the shunting of blood from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs.

While it can cause cyanosis, the clinical presentation usually doesn't include a machinery murmur, and it is typically asymptomatic or mild compared to PDA. Closure of ductus venosus (Option C) occurs normally after birth and redirects blood flow, but it does not cause shunting or significant symptoms like cyanosis or a murmur.

**Malrotation of the great arteries (Option D):** is a form of congenital heart defect that can cause cyanosis, but it would typically be detected earlier, often with profound cyanosis from birth. Unlike PDA, it does not present with a machinery-like murmur and does not involve a left-to-right shunt.

questions.question: In the given CT slice, A and B respectively represent?

options.B: Main bronchus, Descending Aorta
options.C: Ascending Aorta, Descending Aorta

explanation.text: The CT slice is at the level of T5, in which A represents the ascending aorta & B represents descending aorta.

questions.question: The pleural cupola is located:

options.A: Above the diaphragm, covering the lower lung
options.B: Over the apex of the lung, reaching 2 to 3 cm above the clavicle
options.C: Near the midline of the chest at the level of the heart
options.D: At the base of the lungs, covered by the suprapleural membrane

explanation.text: Cervical Pleura Extends from the inner border of the 1st rib. Covers the apex of the lung. Passes downwards and medially to continue with the mediastinal pleura. Pleural Cupola Forms a cup-like dome over the apex of the lung. The summit of the dome reaches 2 to 3 cm higher than the medial third of the clavicle, at the level of the neck of the first rib. Suprapleural Membrane (Sibson’s Fascia) Covers the cervical pleura externally.

A musculo-fascial expansion derived from the scalenus minimus muscle and endothoracic fascia. Extends from the tip of the transverse process of the 7th cervical vertebra to the inner border of the 1st rib. Medially continuous with the pretracheal fascia by the side of the trachea. Relation to Structures All structures related to the apex of the lung are superficial to the suprapleural membrane.

questions.question: Where is pain from the mediastinal pleura typically referred?

options.B: Over the ipsilateral shoulder
options.C: In the lumbar region
options.D: In the lower back near the kidneys

explanation.text: Pleura Structure and Function Visceral Pleura: Surrounds lung tissue. Composed of a single mesothelial cell layer. Blood supply from bronchial arteries. Parietal Pleura: Lines the inner chest wall. Contains stomata that drain pleural fluid into lymphatic capillaries. Connective tissue present; innervated by sensory nerve fibers. Pleural Fluid Normal Volume: 0.1 to 0.2 mL/kg. Inflow Rate: 0.5 mL/hr in adults. Maximal Removal Rate: 0.28 mL/kg/hr.

Accumulates when inflow exceeds removal (due to increased plasma filtration or impaired lymphatic drainage). Lymphatic Drainage Lymph drains into regional lymph nodes along the sternum or vertebra, then into the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts. Lymphatic vessels are 10-12 µm in diameter, large enough for intact erythrocytes. Innervation Visceral Pleura: No connective tissue; innervated by the vagus nerve, insensitive to pain.

Parietal Pleura: Connective tissue; innervated by intercostal nerves and phrenic nerve. Phrenic Nerve: Predominantly innervates the central diaphragmatic region, referred pain to the ipsilateral shoulder. Pleural Membrane Function Allows frictionless movement of the lungs relative to the chest wall during respiration. Inspiration: Negative pressure in the pleural space leads to lung expansion, allowing air to enter the lungs

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the cardiac plexuses?

options.A: The superficial cardiac plexus is located behind the arch of the aorta, in front of the bifurcation of the trachea.
options.B: The deep cardiac plexus receives cardiac branches from the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves, except the inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus nerve.
options.C: The superficial cardiac plexus distributes to the left coronary artery and right anterior pulmonary plexus.
options.D: The deep cardiac plexus is formed only by the superior cervical cardiac branch of the left sympathetic chain.

explanation.text: Cardiac ganglion of Wrisberg, also called the juxta ductal body or the aortico-pulmonary ganglionic mass. Cardiac Plexuses Superficial Cardiac Plexus: Location: Below the arch of the aorta, in front of the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, to the right of the ligamentum arteriosum (Option A) Cardiac Ganglion of Wrisberg: Located close to the ligamentum arteriosum.

Formation: (a) Superior cervical cardiac branch of the left cervical sympathetic trunk. (b) Inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus nerve. Distribution: (Option C) (a) Deep cardiac plexus. (b) Right coronary artery. (c) Left anterior pulmonary plexus. Deep Cardiac Plexus: Location: In front of the bifurcation of the trachea, behind the arch of the aorta.
Formation: (a) Cardiac branches from three cervical and upper 4-5 thoracic ganglia of the sympathetic chains (except the superior cervical cardiac

**branch of the left sympathetic chain) (Option D):** (b) Cardiac branches from the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves (except the inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus nerve) (Option B) Distribution: Right and left halves of the plexus: (a) Corresponding coronary arteries. (b) Pulmonary plexus. (c) Separate branches to the atria. The illustration below shows Deep cardiac plexus

questions.question: An axial CT scan of the thorax shows a slice where the aortic arch is visible, along with the trachea bifurcating into the main bronchi. At which anatomical level is this axial section most likely taken?

options.B: T3-T4
options.C: T5-T6

explanation.text: At this level, the aortic arch is usually seen, and the trachea begins to bifurcate into the right and left main bronchi. Level of the Thoracic Inlet: This is at the top of the thoracic cavity, where the trachea and esophagus enter. Level of the Aortic Arch: Located around the T4-T5 vertebral level, where the aorta arches over the left main bronchus.

Level of the Carina: At the T5-T6 level, this is where the trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi. Level of the Heart: The heart is typically seen from T6 to T9. You can identify the chambers (right atrium, left atrium, ventricles) and major vessels (aorta, pulmonary arteries).

Level of the Diaphragm: The diaphragm typically corresponds to the T10 vertebral level, which can help in distinguishing between thoracic and abdominal structures. Level of the Esophagus: The esophagus runs along the midline and can be seen at various levels, usually starting from the cervical region down to T10. Level of the Thoracic Spine: The thoracic vertebrae can be used as references; typically, there are 12 thoracic vertebrae.
**T1-T2 (Option A):** This level generally shows the upper mediastinum, including parts of the great vessels, but the aortic arch is not typically prominent.
**T5-T6 (Option C):** Here, the main bronchi are visible, but the aortic arch may not be well-defined.
**T7-T8 (Option D):** This level typically shows the lower mediastinum and may not include the aortic arch or the bifurcation of the trachea.

options.B: Superior vena cava

explanation.text: The left lung shows an impression from the aortic arch, which arches over the left main bronchus. Lung impressions refer to the indentations or impressions made on the surface of the lungs by adjacent structures in the thoracic cavity.

Right lung impressions Left lung impressions Cardiac Impression (Right Atrium & Auricle) Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Impression (Option B) Right Ventricle (Small part) Right Brachiocephalic Vein (Lower part) Azygos Vein Impression (Option D) Esophageal Impression (Option C) Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Impression Tracheal Impression Right Vagus Nerve Impression Right Phrenic Nerve Impression Cardiac Impression (Left Ventricle, Auricle, part of Right Ventricle) Pulmonary Trunk Impression Arch of Aorta Impression Descending Thoracic Aorta Impression Left Subclavian Artery Impression Thoracic Duct Impression Esophageal Impression Left Brachiocephalic Vein Impression Left Vagus Nerve Impression Left Phrenic Nerve Impression Left Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Impression

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient presents with a history of progressive shortness of breath and swelling in the neck. Imaging reveals distended chest wall veins and a mediastinal mass with known metastasis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.B: ) Superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction
options.C: Pulmonary embolism

explanation.text: The presence of distended chest wall veins (collaterals) is highly indicative of increased venous pressure, commonly associated with superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction. In this case, the history of a mediastinal mass and metastasis suggests that the mass is compressing the SVC, leading to venous obstruction.
This obstruction can cause the characteristic collateral circulation (distended chest wall veins) to develop, as the body attempts to reroute blood flow to bypass the obstruction.

**The illustration below shows signs of SVC obstruction Right heart failure (Option A):** While this can cause jugular distension, it typically does not lead to the development of prominent chest wall collaterals without other signs of systemic congestion.
**Pulmonary embolism (Option C):** This may cause acute respiratory distress but does not typically lead to distended chest wall veins or collaterals.

**Thoracic aortic aneurysm (Option D):** This may cause symptoms related to compression of surrounding structures but does not specifically account for the venous distension seen with SVC obstruction.

questions.question: A 56-year-old male patient with a history of gastric carcinoma now presents with sharp or pleuritic pain that worsens with deep breaths or coughing. Pleural effusion is suspected and a pleural tap was done which showed the fluid shown in the image. Based on the knowledge of the course of thoracic duct, where does the thoracic duct drain lymph?

options.B: Into the junction of the left subclavian vein and left internal jugular vein
options.C: Directly into the inferior vena cava

explanation.text: If the pleural effusion fluid is chylous (chyle), it indicates leakage of lymphatic fluid, often due to disruption or injury to the thoracic duct. Chylothorax is a condition where chyle accumulates in the pleural space, leading to pleural effusion. The thoracic duct drains lymph into the junction of the left subclavian vein and left internal jugular vein.

Thoracic duct The thoracic duct starts as the cisterna chyli in the abdomen at the lower border of the T12 vertebra. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm. It initially runs on the right side of the descending aorta in the posterior mediastinum. At the T4 vertebra, it crosses from the right to the left side behind the esophagus. It continues upward along the left border of the esophagus to the root of the neck.

At the root of the neck, it arches laterally at the C7 vertebra, in front of the vertebral arteries and behind the carotid system. The duct collects lymph from the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. It descends in front of the first part of the left subclavian artery.

It ends by draining into the junction of the left subclavian vein and the left internal jugular vein. (Option A, C, & D ruled out) The thoracic duct carries lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, and the left side of the thorax, head, neck, and arm.

questions.question: Which part of the body is not drained by the right lymphatic duct?

options.A: Right side of the head and neck
options.B: Right upper limb
options.C: Right side of the thorax

explanation.text: The right lymphatic duct does not drain the right abdomen; this region is typically drained by the thoracic duct, which handles lymph from the lower half of the body, including the abdomen. Right Lymphatic

Duct The right lymphatic duct may form from the convergence of the right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. These trunks drain lymph from the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right side of the thorax. When present, the right lymphatic duct is approximately 0.5 inches (1.3 cm) long. It opens into the beginning of the right brachiocephalic vein.
Alternatively, the lymphatic trunks may drain directly into the major veins at the root of the neck.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the azygos and hemiazygos veins?

options.A: The azygos vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.
options.B: The inferior hemiazygos vein drains into the superior vena cava.
options.C: The superior hemiazygos vein drains into the azygos vein.
options.D: In an obstruction of the SVC, the superior hemiazygos vein acts as the primary collateral pathway.

explanation.text: The superior hemiazygos vein drains into the azygos vein at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra. Azygos Vein The origin of the azygos vein can vary, often starting from the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein in the abdomen. It ascends through the aortic opening in the diaphragm, on the right side of the aorta. The vein continues to rise until it reaches the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra.

At this level, the azygos vein arches forward above the root of the right lung. It drains into the posterior surface of the superior vena cava. (Option A ruled out) Tributaries: The eight lower right intercostal veins The right superior intercostal vein The superior and inferior hemiazygos veins Mediastinal veins. Pericardial veins Right subcostal vein. Right bronchial vein. Right ascending lumbar vein.

If there is an obstruction of the SVC, the azygos vein acts as the primary collateral pathway to redirect blood from the upper half of the body to the IVC. (Option D ruled out) Inferior Hemiazygos Vein The inferior hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and the left subcostal vein in the abdomen.

It ascends through the left crus of the diaphragm and, around the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra, it turns to the right to join the azygos vein, receiving tributaries from the lower left intercostal and mediastinal veins. (Option B ruled out) Superior Hemiazygos Vein The superior hemiazygos vein is created by the union of the left superior intercostal vein and the fourth to eighth intercostal veins.
It drains into the azygos vein at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the phrenic nerve is false?

options.A: The phrenic nerve contains both motor and sensory fibers.
options.B: Efferent fibers of the phrenic nerve supply the diaphragm muscle.
options.C: Afferent fibers transmit sensory information from the liver capsule.
options.D: Paralysis of the phrenic nerve can result from pressure from malignant tumors in the mediastinum.

explanation.text: Afferent fibers transmit sensory information from both the upper and lower surfaces of the diaphragm, as well as from the pericardium and mediastinal pleura and not from the liver capsule.

Phrenic Nerve The phrenic nerves contain both efferent (motor) and afferent (sensory) fibers. (Option A ruled out) The efferent fibers provide the sole motor supply to the diaphragm muscle. (Option B ruled out) The afferent fibers transmit sensory information to the central nervous system from the peritoneum covering the diaphragm's undersurface, the pleura on the diaphragm's upper surface, and the pericardium and mediastinal parietal pleura.

Paralysis of the phrenic nerve may result from pressure from malignant tumors in the mediastinum. (Option D ruled out) Historically, surgical methods like crushing or sectioning the nerve in the neck were used to treat lung tuberculosis affecting the lower lobes, leading to diaphragm paralysis on that side. This causes the elevated, immobile dome of the diaphragm to provide rest to the affected lung.
